query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: The preservation of structural and chemical stability in near‐equiatomic, multi‐element solid-solution nanoparticles at high service temperatures is governed by the interplay between high configurational entropy and the kinetic barriers imposed by differences in elemental diffusion rates. Nanoparticles designed with a greater mismatch in intrinsic diffusion kinetics among constituent elements will exhibit enhanced resistance to phase segregation and surface elemental segregation under catalytic and thermoelectric conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: Near-equiatomic multi-element solid-solution nanoparticles synthesized by either physical or chemical methods, initially exhibiting a homogeneous dispersion of all elements.
generation.intervention: Tailor the nanoparticle composition to deliberately vary the diffusion rates of the constituent elements (for example, substituting one element with another that has a significantly lower or higher diffusion coefficient) while keeping the overall equiatomic character.
generation.conditions: Exposures at catalytic operation temperatures (773–1173 K) and thermoelectric use temperatures (473–1923 K) under controlled atmospheres representative of service regimes.
generation.structural_mediator: The kinetics of elemental diffusion and resultant surface segregation or phase separation in the nanoparticle lattice.
generation.mechanism: High configurational entropy generally stabilizes the single-phase structure; however, if certain elements diffuse more rapidly than others at high temperatures, local compositional fluctuations trigger phase segregation or surface enrichment effects. By engineering a greater mismatch in diffusion kinetics, kinetic barriers to homogenization are enhanced, thereby preserving the single-phase structure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles with engineered diffusion mismatches among their constituent elements will exhibit less phase segregation (as evidenced by more uniform elemental mapping) and maintain catalytic activity and thermoelectric performance better than nanoparticles with uniformly high diffusion rates under the same high-temperature conditions.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles with equiatomic compositions where the elemental diffusion rates are more balanced, leading to more rapid onset of phase segregation or elemental segregation under high-temperature conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies only to service conditions where the temperatures are sufficiently high to activate diffusion processes but not so high as to cause complete melting or non-equilibrium reactions. The effects are most relevant for nanoparticles synthesized to be near-equiatomic in composition and subjected to prolonged high-temperature exposures in environments that are not excessively oxidizing.
generation.uncertainty: The relative contribution of thermodynamic driving forces versus kinetic factors in determining stability is not fully quantified at the nanoscale; therefore, the exact threshold of diffusion mismatch needed for enhanced stability is uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two series of nanoparticles: one series with intentionally engineered high diffusion mismatch through elemental substitution (while keeping overall equiatomic composition) and a control series with balanced diffusion properties. Expose both series to identical catalytic (773–1173 K) and thermoelectric (473–1923 K) operating conditions. Monitor structural evolution using in-situ high-resolution microscopy and elemental mapping (e.g., TEM-EDS), complemented by phase identification via X-ray diffraction.
measurements: In-situ TEM and TEM-EDS elemental mapping
Catalytic activity and thermoelectric performance assessments over time
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no significant difference in phase segregation, elemental surface enrichment, or performance degradation is observed between the high diffusion mismatch series and the control series under the prescribed conditions, then the hypothesis that engineered diffusion mismatch is critical for enhancing structural and chemical stability is falsified.
